units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

narration_plan.release: not generated yet (generate right before publication)

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Hash every integer lattice point to a unit gradient, make the surface zero there with that slope, and blend the four corner planes with the quintic fade 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 so slope and curvature join across cells: a smooth, bounded, stateless texture at any point and scale, with octaves at halving amplitude for terrain.
units.description: Perlin noise on a 256 x 256 lattice: exactly 0 at 16,384 of 16,384 grid points with the hashed slope; inside the sqrt(2)/2 bound on 265,536 samples, attained in 28 cells; border slope jump 2.7e-9 (quintic) against 2.703 (linear crease); curvature step 12.5 for the 1985 cubic; 0.005% of the power above two cycles per cell.
units.time: O(2^n) corner gradients per sample (4 in 2D)
units.baseline: Value noise (random lattice heights, same fade)
units.plan_row: Perlin noise × Gradient lattice interpolation. Puzzle 191, signal-graphics (problemSlug procedural-texturing, the atlas problem page carrying "Procedural texturing"; atlas topic graphics-rendering, tier 1; first live unit of that topic). Solution perlin_noise_gradient_lattice_interpolation.py (0.5s, prints OK): a seeded Lattice class (permutation of 0 to 255 written twice, hash p[p[i & 255] + (j & 255)], eight unit gradients or a value in [-1, 1] per grid point, a corner-fetch counter as the work currency), 2-D Perlin noise with a pluggable fade (quintic 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3, Perlin's 1985 cubic 3t^2 - 2t^3, linear), value noise on the same lattice, white noise with one hash per sample, fractal Brownian motion, 2-D simplex noise, a recursive FFT, and helpers for power bands, median frequency, lag-one autocorrelation, zero crossings, and one-sided slope and curvature jumps. ORACLES: (1) exactly 0.0 at 16,384 of 16,384 lattice points; the central-difference slope there equals the hashed gradient to 1.0e-7, root-mean-square slope 1.000000 for Perlin against 5.7e-8 for value noise (every grid point of value noise is a stationary point); (2) the range bound sqrt(2)/2 = 0.707107 held at all 65,536 cell centers of the torus and 200,000 random points, attained exactly in 28 cells (5 with all four gradients pointing inward, 23 outward); mean -0.0007, standard deviation 0.2104; (3) across 2,000 cell borders the one-sided slope jump is 2.70e-9 (quintic), 8.13e-5 (cubic), 2.703 (linear, a crease; interior slopes reach 1.860), value noise 3.6e-9, simplex at random points 3.6e-4; the curvature jump is 0.1241 at h = 1e-3 and 0.0125 at 1e-4 for the quintic (shrinking: continuous curvature) against 12.4533 and 12.5148 for the cubic (a step: the 2002 improvement); (4) FFT of 4,096 samples (16 per cell) along lattice-periodic lines: Perlin on a generic line 41.7% of the power below a quarter cycle per cell, 58.3% between a quarter and two cycles, 0.005% above two, median frequency 0.301 cycles per cell, lag-one autocorrelation 0.9871, 0.82 zero crossings per cell; along a lattice row 6.1% / 93.9% / 0.010%, median 0.512; value noise 58.3% / 41.7% / 0.002%, median 0.199, lag-one 0.9929, 0.51 crossings; white noise 0.6% / 19.4% / 80.068%, median 4.000, lag-one -0.0658, 8.50 crossings; (5) corners per sample Perlin 4 against simplex 3 (simplex range [-0.705, +0.706] after its x70 scale); four octaves at halving amplitude inside the bound with standard deviations 0.2104, 0.1560, 0.1371, 0.1288 (max +0.6409, +0.4753, +0.4320, +0.4085). Two author corrections recorded in the file header: the draft wrote the range as [-1, 1] (the scaled range) where the raw bound is sqrt(2)/2, and the draft called the noise band-pass where a generic line carries two fifths of its power below a quarter cycle per cell (band-pass only along a lattice row), so the page says band-limited above. Cards: self, Simplex noise, Worley noise, Diamond-square algorithm (all algoName; pages verified in dist/algo). Baseline: value noise. neverUse: linear interpolation in place of the fade (the 2.703 crease), with white noise as the other trap. Contest table: six rows (quintic, cubic, linear, value noise, white noise, simplex) over grid-point behavior, border slope jump, power above two cycles per cell, median frequency, corners per sample. Figure: one-dimensional gradient noise across twelve cells (green zeros, blue hashed slopes, amber quintic blend, dashed red linear blend with creases), the three fades described in the caption; cite Perlin 1985 SIGGRAPH DOI 10.1145/325165.325247 and Perlin 2002 Improving Noise DOI 10.1145/566654.566636. Viz PerlinNoiseViz: a ten by four window onto a seeded lattice, one cell blended per tick with the hashed gradients in blue and the quintic-faded value in grey, then three ticks adding octaves two to four; invariant every tick: exactly zero at all 55 lattice points through every octave and every sample inside the scaled bound; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 43 ticks, 0 breaks (501,760 samples per cycle); stepMs 320, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba, plan 24,388 billable characters (12,194 spoken per voice), 8 requests, $0.731640, approval c106075fde32fd9cbf68771828a09dd0b7e9c2d0184d41cfb95c9c47f6af0277 (not generated yet). units.oneLiner: Every router keeps one vector, its best known distance and next hop to each destination, hands it to its neighbors every update interval, and relaxes to the cheapest offer plus the link: Bellman-Ford spread across the routers, settling in L minus one intervals, and counting a dead route up to a finite infinity when a link dies.
units.description: Distance-vector routing against Dijkstra and Floyd-Warshall on 200 random graphs: tables equal on every pair, settled in exactly L − 1 intervals; the failed chain counts 3, 4, 5 … 15 to infinity in 15 intervals where split horizon takes 2; poison reverse still fails the RFC 1058 triangle (565 of 1,000 orders); with no cap, 1,002 and counting.
units.time: O(n) entries per router per update interval to each neighbor; L − 1 intervals to settle, at most n − 2
units.space: O(n) per router: a distance and a next hop per destination
units.baseline: Link-state flooding plus Dijkstra at every router
units.plan_row: Distance-vector routing × Bellman-Ford exchange. Puzzle 193, distributed-systems (problemSlug network-routing, the atlas problem page carrying "Network routing"; sibling live lessons bellman-ford-early-exit, puzzle 34, and dijkstra-binary-heap, puzzle 7). Solution distance_vector_routing_bellman_ford_exchange.py (2.0s, 16,430 bytes, prints OK): a random connected weighted graph generator, a lexicographic (cost, hops) Dijkstra that also counts relaxations, Floyd-Warshall, a BFS hop diameter, a DistanceVector class (lockstep or random asynchronous order; split horizon, poison reverse, triggered updates, infinity cap; counts vectors, entries, and changes including next-hop changes, and the worst transient distance to a watched destination), and a link-state flood followed by a counting Dijkstra per router. ORACLES: (1) 200 random graphs (18.7 routers, 38.4 links): quiet tables equal Dijkstra and Floyd-Warshall on every pair, next hops reach every destination at the referee's cost; busy intervals == L - 1 on 200 of 200 (max L 8, max 7 busy), at most n - 2; DV 5.49 intervals incl. the quiet one, 438 vectors, 9,261 entries per graph, 37 numbers per router; link state floods in exactly the BFS hop diameter (4.14 rounds), 5,794 records, 1,635 relaxations, 114 numbers per router. (2) Chain A-B-C, A-B fails, infinity 16, lockstep: plain 15 intervals, worst 15, 15 changes, trace (3,2),(3,4),(5,4),(5,6)...; split horizon 2 intervals, worst 2 (stale truth); poison reverse 2 / 2; triggered updates 1 interval, worst 15, the same 15 changes (asserted equal); 7.5 minutes at RIP's 30 s; poison reverse over 500 random asynchronous orders: worst 2, no count. (3) RFC 1058 triangle after C-target fails: plain, split horizon, poison reverse all 15 intervals / worst 15 in lockstep (the dead route circles A, B, C one router per interval); 565 of 1,000 random asynchronous orders under poison reverse count to 15 (10.0 intervals each), 435 settle in 2.8. (4) 99 random hop-count meshes losing a router: plain / split / poison all 15.0 intervals and worst 15, entries after the failure 10,626 / 8,789 / 10,626; link state 3.3 flood rounds. (5) No cap: after 1,000 intervals B and C hold (1,001, 1,002) and are still changing. Honest: two AUTHOR CORRECTIONS recorded in the header (the draft expected poison reverse to settle the lockstep triangle in four intervals, the trace showed the dead route circling the three routers to 15, so the page calls poison reverse a two-router fix; and a next-hop change at an unchanged distance now counts as a table change, because under poison reverse it changes what neighbors hear, after a premature quiet left one viz router at infinity). Trimmed to the chunk budget at the coordinator's request: the 100-mesh link-loss sweep was dropped, the estimator reads 18.9 KB (solution 16,430 B, content 16,705 B, narration 12,685 B with 12,047 spoken characters, viz 10,618 B). Cards: self, Link-state routing (algoName), Path-vector routing (algoName), Bellman-Ford (live lesson badge, puzzle 34); all pages verified in dist/algo. neverUse: the vector exchange with no finite infinity on links that fail (1,002 and counting; 15 intervals even with the cap on the chain, the triangle, and 99 of 99 meshes). Contest: 5 rows x 4 columns (intervals to settle, worst distance held, what happens, cost). Figure: the chain's (B, C) staircase to the cap of 16 beside split horizon's drop at intervals 1 and 2; cite Hedrick RFC 1058 (1988) DOI 10.17487/RFC1058, Bellman 1958. Viz DistanceVectorViz: nine routers on a seeded mesh with unit links learn their distance to one amber destination, one lockstep interval per tick, blue next-hop markers, green when equal to a BFS referee; after a three-tick hold a failure strikes (seed-driven variant: destination isolated or one used link cut, plain or poison reverse) and the tables re-route or count the dead route in red to the cap of 16; invariant every tick: estimates at least the truth while building, quiet tables equal the referee (infinity included), build took exactly L - 1 busy intervals, no finite estimate reaches the cap; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks, and 40 seeds with every final ok true across all four variants; stepMs 520, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba (plan 24,362 billable characters, 8 provider requests, $0.730860, approval 6980c209...). units.oneLiner: Count each symbol, divide by n, and plug the frequencies into Shannon's formula: one pass, nothing to tune, and a bias that is always negative and known to first order, (k − 1)/(2n ln 2) bits, so that at ten samples per symbol one added term makes it honest and at one sample per symbol nothing does.
units.description: The plug-in entropy estimator against its exact expectation: bias −0.0728 bits at n = 1,000 for 100 equiprobable symbols (Miller −0.0714), −0.00715 at 10,000, −3.41 at n = 10; Miller-Madow and the jackknife erase it at n ≫ k; a 2,000-symbol tail at n = 2,000 sits 0.583 bits low; independent variables show 0.0587 bits of plug-in mutual information.
units.time: O(n + k) per estimate: one pass over the samples, one over the counts
units.baseline: Compressed size per symbol (Huffman on the counts)
units.plan_row: Shannon entropy estimation × Maximum likelihood plug-in. Puzzle 195, compression-coding (problemSlug entropy-estimation, the atlas problem page carrying "Entropy estimation"; sibling live lesson huffman-frequency-merges). Solution shannon_entropy_estimation_maximum_likelihood_plug_in.py (0.7 s, prints OK, 62 assertions): the plug-in in its log n form, Miller-Madow and jackknife corrections, the EXACT expectation of the plug-in as a sum of binomial terms (a brute force over every count vector on a 4-symbol alphabet at n = 8 agrees to 1e-12: 1.532790 bits against a truth of 1.846439), a Huffman coder on the counts, Zipf distributions, and a plug-in mutual information. ORACLES: (1) 100 equiprobable symbols (6.644 bits): exact bias -3.41 at n = 10 (E[plug-in] 3.233, log2 10 = 3.322), -2.01 at 30, -0.822 at 100 (Miller first-order -0.714), -0.261 at 300, -0.0728 at 1,000 (-0.0714), -0.0239 at 3,000, -0.00715 at 10,000 (-0.00714); Miller-Madow -2.79, -1.40, -0.370, -0.034, -0.0012 (exact -0.00136), -0.0001, -0.0000; jackknife -2.12, -0.83, -0.065, +0.027, +0.0018, +0.0002, -0.0000; sd 0.0101 at 1,000 and 0.0009 at 10,000 (ratio 11.06: the uniform leading variance term vanishes, 1/n). (2) Zipf over 100 symbols (5.310 bits): bias -2.43 at n = 10, -0.663 at 100, -0.0765 at 1,000 (sd 0.0738), -0.0072 at 10,000 (sd 0.0217; ratio 3.40 against root ten 3.16); Miller-Madow -0.0104 and jackknife +0.0031 at 1,000. (3) All 14 Monte Carlo means (120 to 200 reps) within 3 standard errors of the exact expectation, for the plug-in and for Miller-Madow; bias ratios 1,000 against 10,000: 10.17 uniform, 10.66 Zipf; no sample above log2 of the symbols seen (2,480 samples). (4) Code length on a Zipf sample of 10,000: plug-in 5.2808 = ideal code length; Huffman 5.3185; truth 5.3102. (5) Independent 10 x 10 variables, n = 1,000, 300 reps: plug-in mutual information 0.0587 +/- 0.0005 bits, exact expectation 0.0598, first order (kx - 1)(ky - 1)/(2n ln 2) = 0.0584. (6) NEGATIVE EXAMPLE: Zipf over 2,000 symbols (8.115 bits) at n = 2,000: 632 symbols ever seen, plug-in -0.583, Miller-Madow -0.356, jackknife -0.205; at n = 20,000: -0.079, -0.015, +0.005, 1,785 seen. AUTHOR CORRECTION recorded: the draft claimed the spread shrinks like 1/sqrt(n) for every distribution; the uniform case shrinks like 1/n. Cards: self, Miller-Madow correction, Jackknife resampling (Zahl's entropy jackknife), NSB entropy estimator (all algoName pages exist). neverUse: the plug-in reported as unbiased when n is of the order of k. Figure: exact bias curves (plug-in, Miller's formula, Miller-Madow, jackknife) on log axes beside the collapse bars at n = 10 to 1,000 with the log2 n ceiling; cite Shannon 1948 (DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x), Miller 1955, Paninski 2003 (DOI 10.1162/089976603321780272), Nemenman-Shafee-Bialek 2002. Viz EntropyEstimationViz: a seeded 8-to-16-symbol source, the sample growing 15% per tick to 2,000, empirical bars against true outlines, the plug-in and Miller-Madow climbing toward the truth on a log n axis with the gap shaded; invariants per tick (two formula forms agree, estimate <= log2 of symbols seen, non-negative, correction >= raw); NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 44 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 350, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Hash every eleven-base word of the database once, look up the query's words, extend each exact hit along its diagonal without gaps until the score drops forty below its best, and price every segment with Karlin-Altschul statistics: 5,408 cells where Smith-Waterman spends 4,198,400, at the cost of every homolog that kept no exact word.
units.description: BLAST seeding against a Smith-Waterman referee: 74 of 128 planted homologs at zero decoys in 5,408 cells against 4,198,400 (776x); all 47 misses share no 11-base word with the query; fitted lambda 0.197 against Karlin-Altschul 0.192, 9.1 chance decoys predicted and 13 seen; w = 15 misses 40 of 41 divergent homologs, w = 4 fires 20,101 hits.
units.time: index once; per query O(hits x extension length)
units.space: one index entry per database position
units.plan_row: BLAST × Seed-and-extend word matches. Puzzle 196, comp-bio (problemSlug sequence-database-search, the atlas problem page carrying "Sequence database search"; sibling live lesson smith-waterman-zero-floor, puzzle 56, is the referee). Solution blast_seed_and_extend_word_matches.py (1.5 s, prints OK): word index, ungapped X-drop extension, a search counting hits, extensions, and cells, Smith-Waterman with linear gaps, banded Smith-Waterman around a seed diagonal, the exact best ungapped segment over every diagonal, a Gumbel fit by moments, and a solver for the Karlin-Altschul lambda. Instance: a query of 80 bases against 328 sequences of 160 (200 random decoys, 128 planted homologs, 16 per divergence from 5% to 40%, with indels); +5/-4, gap -6, X-drop 40; thresholds one above the best decoy for every method (zero false positives on the 200 decoys). ORACLES: every HSP recounts from its extents and never exceeds the Smith-Waterman score or the exact ungapped maximum of its pair; Smith-Waterman finds every homolog to 25% and at least as many as seeding at every level (121 of 128 in all); sensitivity falls from w = 7 (105) to 11 (74) to 15 (54); the gapped stage (74) sits between the ungapped search and the referee; two-hit extends less (31 against 92 extensions, 31 found); w = 4 fires more than ten times the hits (20,101 against 1,144; 410,736 cells against 5,408; 10x against 776x); w = 11 spends under a hundredth of the referee's 4,198,400 cells; fitted lambda 0.197 within 30% of Karlin-Altschul 0.192 (K 0.1540, 500 fresh null sequences); at T2 = 54 the fit predicts 9.1 chance decoys and 13 appear, within 2.5 sigma; no decoy admitted by any method (ungapped T = 66 with fitted E-value 1.44 per search, gapped T = 107); the same top hit (sequence 25, 10% divergence); all 75 banded scores equal the full Smith-Waterman score (102,000 cells); every one of the 47 w = 11 misses shares no eleven-base word with the query (0 weak segments, 0 short extensions); 69 of 74 HSPs equal the exact best ungapped segment. Sensitivity by divergence (SW / w7 / w11 / w15): 5%: 1 1 1 1; 10%: 1 1 .94 .94; 15%: 1 1 .88 .62; 20%: 1 1 .75 .56; 25%: 1 .94 .44 .19; 30%: .94 .69 .38 0; 35%: .94 .75 .19 .06; 40%: .69 .19 .06 0. Three author corrections recorded in the header (completeness claim, threshold rule, null construction). Cards: self, FASTA search, Smith-Waterman (live lesson badge), BWA-MEM (all algoName, pages exist). neverUse: a word size tuned for one regime used in another (w = 15 misses 40 of 41 at 30%+; w = 4 explodes). Figure: sensitivity curves by divergence beside a log-scale bar chart of cells; cite Altschul et al. 1990 (DOI 10.1016/S0022-2836(05)80360-2), Karlin and Altschul 1990, Altschul et al. 1997. Viz BlastViz: a dot plot of a 36-base query against a 72-base subject with a planted copy at 10 to 30% divergence, one 7-base word looked up per tick, hits in amber, ungapped extensions in blue, the best HSP in green at the end, counters for hits, extensions, and cells against the full matrix, Smith-Waterman computed up front; invariant: every HSP recounts and never exceeds Smith-Waterman; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 30 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 450, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba. units.oneLiner: Put a Gaussian prior over whole functions, condition it on the data with one Cholesky factorization, and read off a mean and a variance at every input: the squared-exponential kernel supplies the smoothness and one length scale, the marginal likelihood from the same factor chooses the scale, and the error bar is checked against functions drawn from the prior.
units.description: GP regression with the RBF kernel: interpolation to 1e-6; weights equal kernel ridge to 1.4e-8 and the weight-space Bayesian posterior to 3.7e-14; the 95% interval covers 0.9501 ± 0.0057 of 150 prior draws; marginal likelihood recovers the length scale 29 of 30 times; RMSE 0.162 vs 0.266 (3-NN), 0.687 (ℓ = 0.1), 0.626 (ℓ = 8); 182 ms at n = 320.
units.time: O(n^3) once, O(n) per predictive mean, O(n^2) per predictive variance
units.space: the n x n Cholesky factor
units.plan_row: Gaussian process regression × RBF kernel. Puzzle 197, ml-ai (problemSlug regression, the atlas problem page carrying "Probabilistic regression"; topic gaussian-processes, tier 1). Solution gaussian_process_regression_rbf_kernel.py (1.2 s, prints OK): pure Python 1-D GP with our own Cholesky, triangular solves, Gauss-Jordan inverse and determinant, prior sampler, random Fourier features, and a DTC sparse approximation. ORACLES: (1) noise-free interpolation: max |mean - y| 1e-6, max variance 1e-10 at 30 training points; (2) GP weights equal kernel ridge regression (ridge = noise variance 0.04) by Gauss-Jordan to 1.4e-8; (3) quadratic-feature kernel: GP posterior equals weight-space Bayesian linear regression, mean 3.7e-14, variance 6.1e-16; (4) random Fourier features: kernel error 0.1327 / 0.0391 / 0.0470 / 0.0114 and posterior-mean RMSE vs exact 0.1424 / 0.1457 / 0.0602 / 0.0264 at D = 50 / 200 / 800 / 3,200 (not monotone step by step; asserted first-to-last by a factor of three); (5) calibration over 150 prior draws (grid of 51, 20 training, 31 test, noise 0.2): latent 95% coverage 0.9501 ± 0.0057, noisy 0.9486; (6) Cholesky LML -4.422299 equals the direct determinant-and-inverse formula; maximizing over 11 length scales on 30 draws at true ℓ = 1: geometric mean 1.009, 29/30 within one grid step; held-out RMSE ℓ = 0.1: 0.687, ML: 0.162, ℓ = 8: 0.626, 3-NN: 0.266; (7) fit time 1 / 4 / 25 / 182 ms at n = 40 / 80 / 160 / 320, slope 2.87 (160 to 320), n = 10,000 extrapolates to 1.5 h and an 800 MB matrix at this pace; DTC at n = 200 with m = 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 inducing points: RMSE vs exact mean 3.3e-1 / 1.8e-1 / 1.7e-4 / 5.4e-8 at work ratio 0.004 / 0.015 / 0.060 / 0.240. AUTHOR CORRECTION recorded in the header: the draft asserted a monotone random-feature error; measured kernel error rose from D = 200 to 800. Cards: self, Kernel ridge regression, Sparse Gaussian process (DTC), Random Fourier features (all algoName, pages exist). neverUse: a hand-set length scale (0.687 / 0.626 against 0.162; 3-NN at 0.266 beats both). Baseline 3-NN. Figure: held-out RMSE bars for ℓ = 0.1, evidence, 8, and 3-NN beside the DTC gap on a log scale with work ratios; cite Rasmussen and Williams 2006, Krige 1951, Matheron 1963 (DOI 10.2113/gsecongeo.58.8.1246), Neal 1996. Viz GaussianProcessViz: one noisy point per tick (24 per cycle), Cholesky refit, blue mean and 95% band, dashed truth; invariants: variance never negative, never rises when a point is added, Cholesky weights equal Gauss-Jordan to 1e-6; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 23 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Treat a graph as charges and springs: every pair repels by k squared over d, every edge pulls by d squared over k with k the ideal edge length, each vertex moves along its net force by at most a temperature that cools linearly to zero, and the resting positions are the drawing: adjacent near, everything else apart, symmetry recovered because the forces carry it.
units.description: Force-directed graph drawing against crossing counts, edge evenness, and a scale-free stress: a 6 x 6 grid from 522 crossings and stress 0.3372 to 0 and 0.0135 in 126,000 pair forces (Kamada-Kawai 0.0125, spectral 0.0166); a 12-cycle convex ten of ten; cooling 3.517 to 0.099 per iteration; the grid-cell cutoff left 114 crossings; K8 at 56 vs 19.
units.time: O(n² + m) per iteration for a fixed number of iterations
units.space: positions and one displacement per vertex
units.plan_row: Fruchterman-Reingold × Force-directed placement. Puzzle 198, graphs (problemSlug graph-layout, the atlas problem page carrying "Graph layout"; sibling live lessons barnes-hut-octree-center-of-mass-approximation 112, annealing-cooling 2). Solution fruchterman_reingold_force_directed_placement.py (1.7 s, prints OK): seeded graph generators (grid, cycle, path, random tree, ring with chords, complete), random and circular layouts, FR on the free plane (k = sqrt(1/n), repulsion k^2/d over all pairs or within grid cells of side 2k, attraction d^2/k, cap t from 0.1 linearly to 0 over 200 iterations), Kamada-Kawai (springs L d_ij, stiffness 1/d_ij^2, one Newton step per vertex per sweep, 60 sweeps), spectral layout (Hall 1970, two Laplacian eigenvectors by deflated power iteration), referees: segment-intersection crossing count, edge-length CV, scale-free stress 1 - cos^2(euclidean, graph distance), cycle convexity, mean corner error at degree-4 vertices. MEASURED: C12 from ten random starts convex and crossing-free 10/10, edge CV mean 0.004 max 0.005, random starts average 13.3 crossings; 5x5 grid unfolded 9/10 random starts, mean corner error 1.5 deg, edge CV 0.090 on the unfolded ones, the circular start left 11 crossings; P12 straightness 0.977 mean, 0.781 min. Quality table, 6x6 grid (36 v, 60 e): random 522 crossings / CV 0.452 / stress 0.3372; circular 135 / 0.703 / 0.2088; FR 0 / 0.110 / 0.0135, 126,000 pair forces, ~46 ms; Kamada-Kawai 0 / 0.012 / 0.0125, 2,160 Newton steps, ~20 ms; spectral 0 / 0.277 / 0.0166, ~17 ms. Random tree n=40: random 235/0.323/0.3227, circular 152/0.587/0.2893, FR 0/0.398/0.0406, KK 0/0.130/0.0305, spectral 0/1.002/0.0666. Ring n=40 + 6 chords: random 313/0.433/0.2874, circular 3/1.466/0.1453, FR 5/0.253/0.0627, KK 2/0.142/0.0528, spectral 8/0.694/0.1034. C40: random 280/0.407/0.3707, circular 0/0/0.0147, FR 1/0.129/0.1604, KK 0/0/0.0147, spectral 0/0/0.0147. Cooling on the 6x6 grid: displacement per iteration 3.517 (first ten) -> 0.09864 (last ten), energy 33.25 -> 5.09 decreasing on 59% of iterations; NEGATIVE no cooling: last-ten displacement 3.600, stress 0.0164, CV 0.235, 0 crossings. Determinism bitwise; circular start on the 6x6 grid: stress 0.1274, 16 crossings. Grid-cell variant at n = 144, 200 iterations: exact 2,059,200 pair forces, ~417 ms, stress 0.0310, 4 crossings; cells 320,227 pair forces, ~106 ms, stress 0.1448, 114 crossings; bucketed repulsion differs from the exact sum by 77.2% of its norm at the random start; 10,296 pairs per iteration, ~5e11 at a million vertices. NEGATIVE dense graphs: K6 10 crossings (min 3, convex 15), K8 56 (min 19, convex 70). AUTHOR CORRECTIONS recorded in the file: the frame clamp (convex 1/10 at CV 0.2 -> free plane 10/10 at 0.005); FR does not beat the circular layout on the 40-cycle (circle optimal); final moves are cap-bound near 3%, not under 1%. Cards: self (Fruchterman-Reingold), Kamada-Kawai, Spectral layout, ForceAtlas2 (all algoName, pages in dist/algo). neverUse: exact all-pairs repulsion at a million vertices or a hard distance cutoff instead (10,296 pairs/iteration at 144, 5e11 at 1e6; the cutoff dropped 77.2% of repulsion and left 114 crossings vs 4). Figure: the two force curves balancing at d = k beside a stress bar chart of the five grid layouts with crossing counts; cite Fruchterman and Reingold 1991 DOI 10.1002/spe.4380211102, Eades 1984, Kamada and Kawai 1989. units.oneLiner: Give every key one home by hashing it and taking the remainder modulo the shard count: loads as even as a multinomial, no directory, one machine per lookup, and a bill that comes due only when N changes, when the modulo re-homes N/(N + 1) of the data where a ring or jump hash moves 1/(N + 1), and when one hot key needs a salt because no hash can split it.
units.description: Hash partitioning on 16 shards held to the multinomial: chi-square 15.06 against 15 over 100 key sets, heaviest shard 1.09 × mean, 100,000 keys each on one shard at 0.34 µs per route; growing to 17 re-homed 94.2% of keys (theory 94.1%) against 6.4% on a ring and 6.0% with jump hash; a hot Zipf key put its shard at 2.58 × mean until salted (1.19).
units.time: O(1) per route (one hash, one modulo); O(n · N/(N + 1)) keys moved when a shard joins
units.space: O(1) routing state; O(n/N) keys per shard
units.baseline: Range partitioning on the same key
units.plan_row: Sharding × Hash partitioning. Puzzle 199, data-retrieval (problemSlug sharding, the atlas problem page carrying "Horizontal scaling"; sibling live lessons consistent-hashing-virtual-nodes, puzzle 40, and rendezvous-highest-random-weight, puzzle 61). Solution sharding_hash_partitioning.py (2.3 s, prints OK, 21 assertions): a deterministic 64-bit BLAKE2 digest as the hash, the modulo router, a consistent-hashing ring with virtual nodes, jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach 2014), a load counter, and a repeated balance experiment. ORACLES: (1) balance: 100 random key sets of 20,000 keys on 16 shards, chi-square mean 15.06 +/- 0.55 against the multinomial's 15, per-shard sd 33.7 against sqrt(n/N (1 - 1/N)) = 34.2, heaviest shard 1.089 x mean at worst (five-sigma bound asserted); (2) routing: 100,000 keys, loads 6,122 to 6,390 around 6,250, every key found on its home shard and on no other, 0.34 us per route; (3) growth: 16 -> 17 under modulo moves 0.9418 (theory 16/17 = 0.9412, asserted within 0.005), 4 -> 5: 0.804, 8 -> 9: 0.896, 32 -> 33: 0.969 (each within 0.012 of N/(N+1)); doubling 16 -> 32 moves 0.4993 and every mover goes to s + 16; the ring with 100 virtual nodes moves 0.0637 and jump consistent hash 0.0596 (theory 1/17 = 0.0588), every move onto the new node; ring loads after the add 5,290 to 7,113 around 5,882; one point per node leaves the heaviest node at 2.1 to 5.4 x mean over 20 rings; on a 10 TB cluster the modulo moves 9.42 TB against 0.60; (4) skew: 200,000 Zipf requests over 100,000 keys, the hottest key 16,610 requests (8.3%) against a shard mean of 12,500, heaviest shard 2.582 x mean, salting the 13 keys above 1,250 requests into 16 sub-keys each gives 1.190 x; (5) range partitioning: a 1,000-key scan touches 1.013 shards against 16 under hashing, the last 10,000 time-ordered inserts land 100% on one range shard against 7.0% on the busiest hash shard, a query by a non-key attribute fans out to 16 either way; (6) negative example: partitioning user ids by their last digit leaves 6 of 16 shards empty with the heaviest at 1.62 x mean. Two author corrections recorded in the header (one-point ring imbalance guessed at two to three times, measured 2.1 to 5.4; salting only two keys left the third-hottest key's shard at 1.4 x, so the page salts every key above a tenth of the mean). Cards: self, Sharding x Range partitioning (algoName Sharding), Consistent hashing x Virtual nodes (live lesson, puzzle 40), Jump consistent hash; neverUse: a bare modulo on a growing cluster or a last-digit hash. Figure: the move fraction N/(N+1) against 1/(N+1) with the measured dots, beside the Zipf shard loads before and after salting; cites Stonebraker 1986, Karger et al. 1997, DeCandia et al. 2007, Corbett et al. 2012, Lamping and Veach 2014. Viz ShardingViz: keys streaming onto 6 to 9 shards under modulo and onto a ring with 48 virtual nodes, one shard joining at half the keys, moved keys flashed red; invariants every tick (every key on exactly one shard in both schemes, the modulo move within six standard errors of N/(N+1), every ring move onto the new shard); NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 66 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 380, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Slide the template over every window and score each by the correlation coefficient of the two pixel sets, mean removed and variance normalized, so any gain or offset in the lighting still scores exactly one at the true match; read each window's mean and variance from two summation tables in four lookups, floor the variance to refuse flat windows, and fit a quadratic around the peak for the sub-pixel position.
units.description: Template matching by normalized cross-correlation: under a random gain and offset NCC finds the planted 12 × 12 patch 24 of 24 times against SSD 8, SAD 6, raw correlation 22; 6 of 6 at noise σ = 80 where SSD finds 1; summation tables replace 404,496 multiplications with 4,096 and match the direct map to 10⁻¹³; 0 of 6 found at 15° of rotation.
units.time: O(positions × template area) for the dot products; O(1) per window for the mean and variance
units.space: two summation tables of the scene plus the score map
units.plan_row: Template matching × Normalized cross-correlation. Puzzle 200, signal-graphics (problemSlug object-detection, the atlas problem page carrying "Pattern localization"; sibling live lessons hough-transform-parameter-space-voting and fft-cooley-tukey). Solution template_matching_normalized_cross_correlation.py (5.9 s, prints OK): texture generator, bilinear warp (shift, rotation, scale), direct per-window scorer returning NCC, SSD, raw correlation, and SAD from shared window sums, two summation tables, a counting radix-2 FFT, Lewis's fast NCC (tables plus FFT numerator), and a 3 x 3 least-squares quadratic sub-pixel fit; 64 x 64 scenes, 12 x 12 pattern planted at a known position, 2,809 candidate positions, seeded. ORACLES: (1) NCC = 1.000000 (within 1e-9) at six exact copies and |NCC| <= 1 on every map (max 1.000000000); exact copies found 24/24 by all four scores; (2) gain 0.4 to 2.5 and offset +-60 on the scene: NCC 24/24, SSD 8/24, SAD 6/24, raw correlation 22/24; (3) additive noise sigma 15/40/80/120: NCC 6,6,6,5 of 6; SSD 6,6,1,0; SAD 6,6,0,1; raw 6,6,2,0; (4) the table-plus-FFT map equals the direct map to 1.2e-13 with its argmax on the plant; direct 404,496 numerator + 404,496 denominator multiplications per match; tables 4,096 (one squared image); FFT numerator 1,441,792 (three 128 x 128 transforms at four real multiplications per complex one), so the FFT costs more than the direct dot products at this size; (5) sub-pixel: integer peak error 0.640 px, quadratic fit 0.314 px over 16 planted fractional shifts; (6) rotation of the planted pattern, hits of 6 (mean peak): 0 deg 6 (1.00), 5 deg 6 (0.98), 10 deg 6 (0.91), 15 deg 0 (0.85), 20 deg 1 (0.76), 30 deg 0 (0.64), 45 deg 0 (0.49); scale 0.8/0.9/1.0/1.1/1.25: 6/6 at every scale; (7) untextured template without the variance floor: 0/6 found, mean peak 0.26; with the floor flagged 6/6; a flat 20 x 20 scene block floors exactly its 81 windows. Three author corrections recorded in the header: the draft assumed the FFT numerator would cut the multiplication count (counters said the opposite); the draft's smooth scenes let chance windows correlate at 0.83 and beat half-pixel-shifted plants (scenes given finer texture, chance peaks 0.44); the draft's two one-dimensional parabolas (0.61 px) were replaced by the 3 x 3 quadratic (0.36 px on the same seed). Cards: self, Phase correlation, SIFT, Hough transform (live lesson badge), all algoName pages present in dist/algo. neverUse: NCC for a rotated object (6/6 at 10 deg, 0/6 at 15 deg) or a texture-free template (0/6, peak 0.26 without the floor). Contest: 6 rows (NCC tables, NCC direct, NCC FFT numerator, SSD, SAD, raw correlation) x 4 columns (exact copy, gain + offset, noise sigma 80, multiplications per match). Figure: hits under lighting change by score, beside multiplications per match on a log scale; cite Lewis 1995, Briechle and Hanebeck 2001 (DOI 10.1117/12.421129), Brunelli 2009. Viz TemplateMatchingViz: a 40 x 40 scene with an 8 x 8 planted pattern shown under a seeded gain (0.4 to 2.2) and offset (+-60) plus noise, one row of 33 windows scored per tick by NCC and SSD, the NCC map filling in blue, the plant in green, the SSD minimum in amber (wrong in 10 of 40 cycles, NCC right in 40 of 40); invariant every NCC inside [-1, 1] and the final peak on the plant; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 32 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 140, holdTicks rests.
